The scenario catalogue used for release testing covers every hazardous event identified in the hazard analysis and the full operational design domain, as confirmed by independent review.

techniques.name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
techniques.description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team evaluating a vendor's sepsis alert scores a year of its own admissions, plots the ROC curve and fixes the alert threshold its operations committee chose from the vendor's recommended range. At that threshold it reports sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and the share of all admissions that would trigger an alert, and uses the false-positive count and alert volume to decide whether ward staff can act on the alerts.

A card-payments company re-runs the analysis every month on transactions its fraud analysts have labelled, confirms that the false-positive rate at the live threshold is still under the limit agreed with its customer-service team, and, whenever the rate has drifted above that limit, reopens the threshold choice on the latest ROC curve and confirms the new threshold on the following month's labelled sample.

A manufacturer's quality engineers choose the threshold for a visual-inspection model by weighing the cost of scrapping a good part against the cost of shipping a defective one, using the ROC curve and the line's defect rate, then report the false-reject and defect-escape rates that the chosen threshold gives on a separate held-out production batch.

A rail operator's safety team assessing a camera-based obstacle detector for level crossings sets the decision threshold on a tuning set so that the miss rate meets the requirement allocated to the detector. It then measures the false-negative rate at that threshold on a separate set of recorded crossings, broken down into daylight, night and rain, and enters the confusion matrices in the safety case as verification evidence.

limitations.description: The rates are evidence only if they are measured on labelled cases that played no part in choosing the threshold. A threshold set to give a 1 per cent false-positive rate on a tuning set gives exactly that rate there by construction, and with a few hundred negative tuning cases its true rate on new data can be half as high again. Choosing the threshold on one set and reporting rates on another, or nesting the choice inside cross-validation, avoids this at the cost of more labelled data.

False-positive and true-positive rates do not change with how common the positive class is, but the share of alerts that are correct does. A false-positive rate within its limit can still mean most alerts are false when the condition is rare: at 90 per cent sensitivity and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, only about 15 per cent of alerts are correct when 1 case in 100 is positive. Claims about alert burden need the positive predictive value at the deployment prevalence as well.

A rate from a finite test set is an estimate, and with few negatives or few errors it can fall well below the true rate by chance. A claim that a rate is within a limit needs a confidence interval (exact binomial for a single rate; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics for other metrics) narrower than the margin to the limit. With no misses, about 3,000 positives show a miss rate below 1 in 1,000, and 30,000 below 1 in 10,000, at 95 per cent confidence.

The threshold is a fixed score, so the rates hold only while the scores for each class stay as in the test set. A new scanner, fraud pattern or patient mix shifts the scores and moves the false-positive rate with no change to the model, so the analysis must be repeated on labelled operational samples, which can be slow or costly. Labels matter too: where only flagged cases are reviewed, the rate for unflagged cases is unknown unless a random sample of them is labelled.

A single rate averages over the whole test set. It can meet its limit overall while exceeding it for a group of people or an operating condition (night-time images, one hospital site) that is rare in the test data. Rates need reporting for each group and condition the claim covers, each with enough cases to be informative, which can multiply the labelled data required.

resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
techniques.description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

resources.title: Evaluating Frontier Models for Dangerous Capabilities
resources.abstract: To understand the risks posed by a new AI system, we must understand what it can and cannot do. Building on prior work, we introduce a programme of new "dangerous capability" evaluations and pilot them on Gemini 1.0 models. Our evaluations cover four areas: (1) persuasion and deception; (2) cyber-security; (3) self-proliferation; and (4) self-reasoning. We do not find evidence of strong dangerous capabilities in the models we evaluated, but we flag early warning signs. Our goal is to help advance a rigorous science of dangerous capability evaluation, in preparation for future models.

techniques.name: Fault Tree Analysis
techniques.description: Fault tree analysis (FTA) is a deductive, top-down method that starts from one undesired system-level event, such as an automated braking function failing to brake for an obstacle, and works backwards to the combinations of lower-level events that could cause it. The analyst builds a tree of logic gates beneath that top event: an OR gate means any one of its inputs is enough to cause the event above it, an AND gate means all of its inputs must occur together, and the branches end in basic events such as a hardware failure, a human error or a software error. Solving the tree gives its minimal cut sets, the smallest combinations of basic events that produce the top event (a set with a single event is a single point of failure), and, when each basic event has a probability, the probability of the top event, which can be checked against a target or used to set a probability budget for each part. In a system with a machine-learning component, the model's errors enter the tree as basic events of their own, which unlike random hardware failures happen during normal operation at a rate that has to be measured on test or operational data, often depend on conditions such as weather or occlusion that can be added beneath it as conditioning events, and can be correlated from one input to the next. Working down from an acceptable top-event probability turns the model's share into a budget for its error rate, which becomes a performance requirement on the model; the tree shows where model errors matter in the system and how much error it can tolerate, but not why the model makes them.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics team designing an emergency braking system for taxiing aircraft, in which a neural network detects 'No Entry' signs, builds a quantitative fault tree for loss of the restricted-area alert, budgets the detector's misses beside the hardware failures, converts that budget into a maximum per-frame miss probability for the network, and checks on recorded taxi data whether misses in successive frames are independent, as the calculation assumes.

A driving-automation developer analysing the top event 'object not detected in time' adds weather, occlusion and lighting as triggering conditions beneath the camera detector's miss event. Quantifying the tree with rates measured on its own test drives shows which conditions dominate, and it uses the result to decide where a second sensor is needed before widening the vehicle's operating domain.

A hospital pharmacy planning to add a machine-learning dose checker beside pharmacist review draws a tree for 'harmful overdose reaches the patient', with an AND gate requiring both the checker and the pharmacist to miss the error. The analysis shows the claimed risk reduction holds only if the two misses are independent, so the team plans an audit of whether pharmacists check less carefully once the checker is live.

limitations.description: The tree explains only the top events the analysts choose and the causes they think of. Hazards nobody posed as a top event, and losses that arise from interactions between parts that each worked as specified, do not appear, so a fault tree needs a prior hazard identification to decide which top events matter.

A probability for a model-error event is only as good as the data it was measured on. A miss rate estimated on test data holds for the conditions and input mix in that data and changes when the operating environment shifts, so the top-event probability can be badly wrong in conditions the test set under-represents. The main aerospace safety-assessment guidance gives no method for such performance failures, so each assessment has to justify its own.

Quantifying a tree usually assumes basic events are independent, and machine-learning errors often are not: misses on successive camera frames are correlated, and one condition such as fog can degrade a model and the sensor or person meant to back it up at the same time. Unmodelled dependence makes an AND gate look far more protective than it is, so dependence must be checked on data or modelled explicitly.

The model appears in the tree as one or a few basic events, so the analysis says how often the model may err and where its errors matter, not why it errs or which inputs cause the errors. The triggering conditions added beneath a model-error event are only those the analysts already suspect, and finding others needs analysis of the model and its data.

Building and maintaining a tree for a large system is laborious, and it must be revised whenever the architecture or the model changes. Quantification needs a probability for every basic event, and for software, human and model events those numbers are often unavailable or disputed; aviation software guidance, for example, does not accept software reliability rates in the system safety assessment.

techniques.name: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
techniques.description: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (ML FMEA) applies the process form of failure mode and effects analysis, a long-established worksheet method in which a team lists what could go wrong at each step of a process, rates each failure and acts on the worst first, to the pipeline that produces a machine-learning model rather than to the model alone. The team works through the pipeline one step at a time (in the 2025 reference version: collect data requests, collect data, ingest data, validate data, preprocess data, train, tune, analyse, deploy and validate the model, and analyse feedback from the field) and, prompted by guide words such as missing, incorrect or too late, records for each step how the resulting model could fail, the effect on the wider system, the pipeline causes, and the current practices that would prevent or catch the failure. Each row is rated for severity, occurrence and detection, and the product of the three, the risk priority number, ranks the rows so that recommended actions and owners go to the highest risks first; severity is taken from the system-level hazard analysis, because the harm a model failure can do depends on the system it sits in. The method's authors publish a pre-populated template listing typical failure modes, causes and mitigations for each step, which a team tailors to its own model and application. The result is a worksheet of ranked pipeline failure modes, their controls and assigned actions, kept up to date as the pipeline changes; it looks at failures one at a time in how the model is built and does not by itself analyse how the deployed system behaves.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous-trucking company's perception team fills in the template for its lane-detection model before each major retraining. One row under 'collect data' records that data gathered in a single season could leave the model unable to see faded or snow-covered markings; its severity comes from the vehicle-level hazard analysis, and it leads to an action, with an owner and a date, to constrain data requests by season and weather before release.

A medical-imaging company preparing a chest X-ray triage model for regulatory review uses the worksheet to show its assessors where the pipeline's controls sit. High-ranked rows include training labels taken from a single radiologist's reading, which could teach the model to miss small nodules, mitigated by double reading of a labelled sample, and online learning in deployment, mitigated by switching it off.

After a warehouse robot's object detector starts misclassifying a new kind of shrink-wrapped pallet, the vendor's safety engineer returns to the worksheet, finds that the 'analyse model feedback' step had no control for new packaging reaching customer sites, adds drift monitoring and a trigger for new data requests, and re-rates the affected rows.

limitations.description: It considers one failure mode at a time, step by step, so it does not show how failures in different steps combine, or how a model that meets its specification can still contribute to an accident through its interaction with people and other parts of the system. Teams that need those combinations and interactions have to pair it with a system-level analysis.

Severity, occurrence and detection are judgements on ordinal scales, and there is little data on how often an ML pipeline failure occurs or how reliably a control catches it. The method's authors introduced ML-specific rating criteria in 2026 because traditional FMEA criteria proved ambiguous for ML development; the public template, last updated in April 2025, has no rating criteria, so teams must set and record their own.

It analyses how the model is built, not how it behaves in use: a complete worksheet shows that known pipeline failure modes have controls, not that the deployed model performs safely. Severity has to come from a system-level hazard analysis, so the method cannot stand alone, and its authors present it as one part of a safety management system and safety case.

The pre-populated template makes a quick start but invites teams to tick through the listed failure modes instead of looking for ones specific to their system. Its examples come mostly from autonomous-vehicle development, so teams in other domains, or with other kinds of model such as language models, must add their own failure modes; the 2026 revision added steps for problem definition and for building ground truth or reward signals.

Published evidence that the method finds failures other methods miss is limited. The 2025 paper that introduced it gave no applied example, and the 2026 follow-up reporting applications to autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots is led by the method's originators: four of its twelve authors, including the first author, wrote the 2025 paper, so no independent group has yet reported using it.

techniques.name: System-Theoretic Process Analysis
techniques.description: System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is a hazard analysis method developed by Nancy Leveson at MIT that treats safety as a control problem: a loss can occur when parts of a system that have not failed interact unsafely, for example when a controller acts on a wrong belief about the process it controls. The analysis has four steps: define the losses to prevent and the system-level hazards that lead to them; model the system as a control structure of controllers, the control actions they issue and the feedback they receive; identify unsafe control actions; and write loss scenarios explaining how each could arise. An unsafe control action is one of four types (not providing an action causes a hazard, providing it causes a hazard, providing it too early, too late or in the wrong order, or stopping it too soon or applying it too long), and loss scenarios cover causes such as missing or wrong feedback, a flawed control algorithm, or a controller's process model (its internal picture of what it controls) that no longer matches reality. In a system with machine-learning components, a learned model appears in the control structure as a controller whose control algorithm and process model were learned from data, or as a feedback source, such as a perception model, whose errors mislead a controller; loss scenarios include training data that missed an operating condition, a shift from training to deployment conditions, and operators who over-rely on the model, and published adaptations also model data collection, training and evaluation as control loops, so that a scenario can trace an unsafe control action back to a development decision such as an incomplete reward function. The output is a traceable set of unsafe control actions, loss scenarios and the safety constraints and requirements derived from them, which the team uses to change the design and to decide what to test; it analyses a model of the system before or alongside testing, and it gives no probabilities.

example_use_cases.description: An automotive supplier building a pedestrian collision-avoidance function around a neural-network detector models the vehicle's control structure with the detector as the braking controller's source of feedback. It finds the unsafe control action 'emergency braking not applied while a pedestrian is crossing', with scenarios such as missed detections of partly hidden pedestrians at dusk, and turns them into requirements on training-data coverage and on the detector's miss rate.

A hospital's patient-safety team preparing to deploy a machine-learning early-warning score for patient deterioration models the score, the nurses who receive its alerts and the doctors who act on them as one control structure. It finds unsafe control actions such as an escalation that comes too late because vital signs reach the record in batches, and alerts ignored after repeated false alarms, and changes data entry and the alerting rules before go-live.

A frontier AI developer's safety team analysing internal use of an AI coding agent models the engineers who prompt it, the automated monitor that scores its sessions, the human reviewers and the merge gate as controllers of the company codebase. It finds unsafe control actions such as a monitoring alert that arrives after the agent's change has been merged, and sets requirements on how quickly sessions are reviewed and on reviewers' independence from the agent.

An engineering team training a reinforcement-learning policy to land a drone splits the mission into approach, descent and touchdown, identifies unsafe control actions for each phase, such as descending too fast close to the landing pad, and uses the loss scenarios to choose the wind and sensor-noise perturbations for its simulation tests and to adjust the reward before the next round of training.

limitations.description: The analysis depends on judgement at every step: deciding which losses matter, where the system ends, which parts act as controllers and which scenarios to record. Separate teams analysing the same system can reach different models and scenario lists, so the work needs review by people outside the team, and a short list of loss scenarios is not evidence that no others exist.

STPA does not estimate how likely a hazard or scenario is, and its authors argue that such estimates are unreliable for software-intensive systems. Where an assurance case or regulator needs a quantitative target, such as a failure rate per hour, it must be paired with a quantitative method, and STPA alone cannot show that a scenario is too rare to need a mitigation.

For a learned component the analysts cannot read the process model or the control algorithm, because both are encoded in trained weights. Scenarios explaining why the model would act unsafely are therefore hypotheses about its training data and operating conditions until tests or monitoring confirm them, and for policies with continuous states and actions the analysis has to be split by mission phase or subtask to stay manageable.

A control structure that covers only the system in operation misses causes that lie in how the model was built, such as data collection, labelling, reward design or the choice of evaluation set; a survey of 31 studies applying STPA to learning-enabled systems found that most modelled operation only. Adding the development lifecycle as control loops finds these causes but makes the analysis substantially larger.

A full analysis of a complex system takes sustained effort from people trained in the method, working with domain and machine-learning experts. A language model can draft loss scenarios faster, but its drafts steer the team towards the scenarios it happens to suggest and can leave gaps, so they need the same review as scenarios written by hand.

techniques.name: Linear Bound Propagation Verification
techniques.description: Linear bound propagation verification proves that a trained neural network meets a stated property for every input in a defined region, for example that no small change to the pixels of an image alters its class, or that a controller's output stays within limits across a box of sensor readings. CROWN, the named method, replaces each neuron's activation function with two straight lines that bound it from above and below over the values that neuron can take, then works backwards from the outputs through the layers to express an upper and a lower bound on each output as a linear function of the input, and evaluates those functions over the region to obtain guaranteed numerical bounds. If the bounds show the property holds (for a classifier, that the correct class's score stays above every other class's), it is proved for the whole region; because the straight lines over-approximate the network, bounds that fail to show it leave the case undecided, so bound propagation on its own is sound but incomplete. The alpha-beta-CROWN tool tightens the bounds by tuning the lines with gradient-based optimisation and by branch and bound: for a ReLU network it splits undecided neurons into their active and inactive cases and bounds each part separately, which given enough time settles every case, making the tool complete for ReLU networks, but at a cost that can grow exponentially with the number of neurons split, so in practice each run ends as verified, falsified (a counterexample input found) or timed out. Running on graphics processors, it reaches convolutional networks with millions of parameters, larger than exact constraint solvers usually handle, at the price of leaving hard cases undecided.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics supplier's verification team checks the network that flags wildfires in airborne infrared images. For each background crop in a held-out set taken from real flight logs, it uses alpha-beta-CROWN to prove that the detector's confidence never falls as a planted fire signal grows stronger within the specified range, lists the crops where a counterexample is found, and enters the proved cases in the safety case as evidence for that consistency requirement.

A transmission system operator replaces slow time-domain simulation with a neural network that predicts whether the grid stays stable after a fault, inside the optimiser that plans generator dispatch. At each candidate dispatch its engineers use alpha-beta-CROWN to certify that the stability prediction holds for every combination of wind, solar and load within the forecast uncertainty, and raise the stability margin wherever certification fails before the plan is issued.

A pharmaceutical packaging line uses a convolutional classifier to accept or reject blister packs from camera images. Before each model release the quality team reports certified accuracy on held-out images: the share for which CROWN bounds prove that no change of up to 2/255 in any pixel can flip the decision, a bound set above the largest per-pixel noise measured on the line's cameras. A release whose certified accuracy falls well below its ordinary accuracy goes back for retraining.

limitations.description: Bound propagation on its own is incomplete: when the bounds are too loose to show the property, the case stays undecided, which is not evidence either way. Branch and bound settles more cases, but the problem is NP-complete in general, so hard cases end in a time-out. In an industrial study of an airborne wildfire detector, every query for a monotonicity property was settled, while 62 per cent of the queries for a sensor-blur property timed out.

The property must be written as a region of inputs, such as every image within a small per-pixel change of a test image or a box of sensor values, plus a linear condition on the outputs. Rotation, lighting, weather or blur are not regions of that kind; covering them means modelling them first, for example with a separate network that generates plausible blur, and the accuracy of that model then has to be argued separately.

Robustness is proved one region at a time, usually around each test input, so certified accuracy on a test set is evidence about those inputs and that perturbation only. It does not carry over to new inputs from operation, and a classifier certified around every test image can still misclassify an unperturbed image it has not seen.

It needs the whole network in a supported form (PyTorch or ONNX) and, beyond small networks, a graphics processor with enough memory: most of the tool's example configurations were tested on a 24 GB GPU, and its documented branch-and-bound support for ReLU image models reaches residual networks of about 20 layers. Layers the library does not support need their bounds written by hand, and its documented reach of millions of parameters is far below the size of large language models.

The guarantee covers the network alone. Pre-processing, sensor faults and, for a controller, the plant it drives and how errors build up over time are outside it, so a proof that a policy network never outputs an unsafe command for any state in a box does not show that the controlled system stays safe; that needs a separate analysis of the closed loop.

resources.title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions
resources.abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

techniques.name: Signal Temporal Logic Monitoring
techniques.description: Signal temporal logic (STL) monitoring checks the signals a system produces over time, such as speeds, distances, positions or a model's outputs, against safety requirements written in signal temporal logic, a formal language for stating how real-valued signals must behave over time intervals (for example, 'whenever the gap to the vehicle ahead falls below 10 m, speed drops below 5 m/s within 2 s'). Each requirement is built from comparisons of signals with thresholds, joined by logical operators and by timed operators such as 'always within [a, b]', 'eventually within [a, b]' and 'until'. For each trace the monitor computes a robustness value, a margin to the requirement rather than robustness to adversarial inputs: its sign says whether the requirement is met (positive) or violated (negative), and its size is a tolerance: any signal whose values stay closer than that to the observed ones at every instant gets the same verdict. Monitors run offline on logged or simulated traces, or online on live signals, where a requirement that looks ahead in time can be decided only once enough of the signal has arrived. RTAMT, the named tool, is an open-source Python library with an optional C++ back-end that builds such monitors from a written specification and connects to ROS and MATLAB/Simulink; its online monitors accept only requirements whose future time windows are bounded and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's time horizon, and it reports the robustness value but does not act on it, so stopping or correcting the system is left to a separate safeguard.

example_use_cases.description: A team developing an adaptive cruise controller with a learned speed policy writes its requirements in STL, for example that the time gap to the vehicle ahead never stays below one second for longer than two seconds, and attaches an RTAMT monitor to every drive in an urban driving simulator. The robustness values show which controller settings meet each requirement and by what margin, and drives with negative values become regression scenarios.

A hospital's service robot, which uses learned perception to find people, fetches supplies along corridors. The integrator monitors live ROS topics against a system requirement (always at least 0.5 m from any detected person) and against one requirement per subsystem, such as the planner reaching its next waypoint in time. When a subsystem requirement fails shortly before the system one, the logged verdicts show where the fault began.

A drone-delivery operator checks each day's flight logs from its learned landing controller against a requirement that, in the last ten seconds before touchdown, descent rate stays below 1 m/s and the drone stays within 0.5 m of the pad centre. It reports the smallest robustness value across all landings to its safety manager and investigates any landing whose value is negative.

limitations.description: The monitor checks the requirement as written, not as intended. Writing correct STL needs fluency in the logic and in the system: a wrong threshold, a time window that is too short or a misplaced operator yields confident positive margins for behaviour the engineers would call unsafe, and nothing in the monitor reveals the mistake. Specifications need the same review as the requirements they encode.

Online monitoring judges a requirement from a partial trace. RTAMT's online monitors take only requirements whose future time windows are bounded, and give each verdict after a delay equal to the requirement's horizon: a check that something happens within five seconds is decided five seconds later, which may be too late to act on in a fast system. Monitors that track a narrowing range of possible robustness values can flag some violations sooner, but stay undecided until the data settles it.

A robustness value is measured in the units of the signals in the requirement, so a margin of 0.4 means 0.4 metres in one requirement and 0.4 degrees in another. Values cannot be compared across requirements, and when one requirement combines signals of different scales its value is set by whichever margin is numerically smallest, which depends on the units chosen unless the signals are normalised first.

Monitoring reports on the traces it sees. A clean record over many hours shows that those runs met the requirement, not that every possible run will, and a violation is reported when it happens, not before, unless a separate predictor of future signals is added. To protect the system, the verdict has to drive a safeguard such as a fallback controller, which the monitor does not provide.

The verdict is only as good as the signals. If a learned perception component misjudges the distance to a person, the monitor computes a confident margin from the wrong distance; independent sensors or ground truth are needed to check the perception itself. Discrete-time monitors see only the samples taken, so a brief violation between samples can go unseen, and the ROS integration assumes messages arrive at a known, regular rate.

techniques.name: SMT-Based Neural Network Verification
techniques.description: SMT-based neural network verification decides exactly whether any input in a defined region can make a trained neural network violate a stated property, and if one can, returns that input as a counterexample. SMT (satisfiability modulo theories) solvers decide whether a set of logical and arithmetic constraints can all hold at once: here the network's weighted sums become linear equations, each piecewise-linear activation such as ReLU becomes a constraint with two cases (inactive at zero, or active and passing its input through), and the input region and the negation of the property become further linear constraints. The solver searches for values that satisfy every constraint with a simplex-based linear-programming engine: it first tries to repair an activation whose current values break it, and splits it into its two cases only when repairs keep failing, while bounds on each neuron (in Marabou, by default, the linear bounds that bound propagation computes) rule cases out early. Reluplex (Katz et al., 2017) introduced this lazy treatment of ReLU inside the simplex method and used it on a prototype airborne collision avoidance network; Marabou, its maintained successor, keeps the same search structure with a newer search procedure, adds parallel solving, and can emit a proof certificate for an 'unsatisfiable' answer. The answer is 'unsat', meaning no input in the region violates the property, or 'sat' with a concrete counterexample, and for networks whose activations are all piecewise-linear the procedure is complete; the price is that the number of cases can grow exponentially with the number of neurons, so it is practical for small networks such as controllers, policies and surrogate models with few inputs rather than large image models.

example_use_cases.description: A warehouse robotics team trains hundreds of candidate deep reinforcement learning policies for driving between shelves from range-sensor readings. Before field trials it encodes 'no move into an obstacle in the next step' and 'no repeating left-right loop over several steps' as queries over each small policy network, runs Marabou on every candidate, discards each policy for which a counterexample reading is returned, and takes only the survivors to the physical robot.

An aircraft systems developer replaces a large collision-avoidance lookup table with a set of small neural networks. For each network it writes regions of encounter geometry, such as an intruder close ahead and closing, together with the advisory that must never be issued there, and runs the solver on each. Regions returned as unsatisfiable go into the certification evidence; any counterexample encounter is replayed in simulation and drives retraining.

A medical-device manufacturer uses a small network to recommend infusion rates from a handful of patient measurements. Its safety engineers prove that, for every combination of measurements within the clinically plausible ranges, the recommended rate never exceeds the maximum set by the device's hazard analysis, and use any counterexample returned to retrain the network or add an output limit.

limitations.description: Deciding these queries for ReLU networks is NP-complete, and the search may split on every neuron whose case is undecided, so time can grow exponentially with network size and with the number of steps a property spans. In a study of robot navigation policies kept to 16 neurons per hidden layer, single-step collision queries took seconds, but 12-step cycle queries usually ran for hours and nearly three in ten of them hit the 12-hour limit.

The solver runs on ordinary processors, and its own tool paper reports a non-trivial performance gap to GPU-based bound-propagation verifiers, especially on larger networks; in the 2023 verification competition it solved 594 benchmark instances to alpha-beta-CROWN's 721. It is therefore best suited to small networks with few inputs, such as controllers, policies and surrogate models.

Exact answers hold only for piecewise-linear activations such as ReLU, max, absolute value and leaky ReLU. Sigmoid and tanh are handled by an over-approximation that is refined step by step, and softmax and bilinear layers only through a convex relaxation, so for networks that use them the procedure is no longer complete and can end without a decisive answer.

The query covers the network and a region of its inputs written as linear constraints, nothing more. A counterexample may lie in a part of the region no real sensor could produce, and a proof says nothing about the environment the network acts in, so choosing a region that is realistic yet small enough to solve takes domain knowledge, and a closed-loop safety claim needs further analysis.

An 'unsat' answer is only as trustworthy as the solver's implementation. Marabou can emit a proof certificate that an independent checker validates, but proof production works with only some of its features and not in parallel mode, and in the tool paper's collision-avoidance experiments certificates were produced for 113 of 180 benchmarks.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.
